newsitem.title: CANADA: Scotiabank CEO says drop foreign bank rules.
newsitem.headline: Scotiabank CEO says drop foreign bank rules.

text.p: Barriers to foreign banks operating in Canada, including rules against bank branches, should be dropped, Bank of Nova Scotia chairman Peter Godsoe said on Tuesday.
"On restrictions on foreign banks operating in Canada -- drop them. We have absolutely no concerns about being able to compete successfully," Godsoe told the annual meeting.
Under Canadian rules, a foreign bank must set up a federally regulated subsidiary with its own capital, board of directors and audit system.
A federal policy paper last summer proposed lifting some restrictions on foreign banks, but they must still operate separately capitalized subsidiaries in Canada.
The higher cost of operating a subsidiary compared to a branch has driven several foreign banks out of Canada.

Godsoe said there was a need to ensure that regulations concerning capital, tax and governance policies were reasonably balanced, "but as a matter of general principle, foreign banks should be allowed to open branches in Canada."
Godsoe said he had mixed views on the subject of Canadian bank mergers, which are favored by Scotiabank's bigger rivals.
Royal Bank of Canada, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and Bank of Montreal have said mergers were necessary for Canadian banks to stay competitive internationally.
Federal laws discourage bank mergers by limiting investors to a maximum 10 percent stake in a Canadian bank.

"If mergers are permitted...in my view, we would lose one or two banks -- possibly even three -- to acquisition fairly quickly," Godsoe said. Shareholders would do well, but customer service might decline due to branch rationalization if one or two Canadian banks merged, he said.

"This loss of competition at the local level might also translate into differential pricing schemes, with higher rates and fees in some parts of the country as opposed to others -- a phenomenon we see south of the border," Godsoe said.
He also urged the Canadian government to speed up its review of the financial services sector. The timeline for the review suggests no meaningful action will happen until 2002, Godsoe said.
"By then, Japan and Australia will have completed their financial sector policy reviews, and the United States will have already moved to open up its financial sector," he said.
